 Data centre mooted beside Bohol flood detention pond
 By BAVANI M 
 Photos By Photos: ART CHEN/The Star 
 Monday, 16 Nov 2026
 share 
 bookmark 
 Related Stories
 Letters 
 2h ago 
 Keeping data centres green 
 Sabah & Sarawak 
 14 Nov 2026 
 Strict rules for data centres 
 Nation 
 13 Nov 2026 
 11 data centre projects approved as of October, nine already operational, says Digital Ministry 
 A view of Kampung Bohol Flood Detention Pond from the moon bridge, with landscaping work still underway. The prospect of a data centre in the vicinity has drawn concern from community groups. 
 No formal application yet as community groups seek answers on traffic, utilities and water flow 
 THE mixed-development project on land surrounding Kampung Bohol Flood Detention Pond in Kuala Lumpur may now see a data centre come up in place of private housing.
 This possible development has sparked mixed views, though residents and stakeholders share the call for transparency and public consultation.
 No formal application has been submitted for the possible change, which involves one of three parcels earmarked for private residential development on Lot 102996, near Shah Alam Expressway (Kesas).
 Almost ready: Aerial view of the upgraded Kampung Bohol Flood Detention Pond, which is operational aside from a 2km walking path and park being built around the pond. — FAIHAN GHANI/The Star 
 StarMetro learnt from sources familiar with the matter that the developer was considering a data centre for one or more of the three private residential parcels.
 A spokesperson for the developer confirmed this, saying the idea was at an early stage and that only the plots closest to the highway were being considered.
 ALSO READ:   Pond fully operational, handover end-November 
 “We believe a data centre could generate less traffic and noise than housing, especially as we still have to build the affordable housing components.
 “A condominium would bring hundreds or thousands of new residents and vehicles into the area,” the spokesperson said.
 “The land is still designated for housing, so any change would require the necessary land-use conversion and approvals.
 “Under the land alienation deal, we would also still be required to build the Madani housing and Rumah WIP,” the spokesperson added.
 A senior Kuala Lumpur City Hall (DBKL) officer confirmed that the developer had raised the idea with City Hall.
 “There have been discussions, but nothing has been finalised because no application has been submitted.
 “It is something we will look into when an application is made,” the officer said.
 The officer added that the developer remained obligated to deliver the Rumah WIP and Madani housing components, and was currently focusing on handing over the upgraded flood detention pond and adjoining recreational park to the authorities.
 Kok says preliminary talks on data centre has taken place. 
 When contacted, Seputeh MP Teresa Kok confirmed that preliminary talks have taken place.
 “I have already checked with DBKL about this matter. There have been talks, but no application has been submitted,” she said.
 The 10.83ha land comprises six plots alienated in 2024 for a mixed-development project.
 In return, the developer was mandated to build a flood detention pond and an adjoining park at a cost of RM40mil.
 Plots 1 and 4, measuring 1.92ha each, are earmarked for Rumah WIP affordable housing, while the 1.21ha Plot 6 is intended for Madani affordable housing.
 Plots 2 and 3, measuring 2ha each, and the 1.78ha Plot 5 are earmarked for private condominiums.
 All six parcels are designated for residential use, so any data centre proposal would require a formal land-use conversion application alongside planning and technical approvals.
 Federal Territory of Kuala Lumpur Land and Mines Office (PTGWP) (land registration sector) deputy director Mohd Firdaus Ibaruslan had said on May 16, 2024 that the arrangement was not a land-swap deal.
 “Besides forking out RM40mil to upgrade the pond, the developer still needs to pay RM41.7mil in premium for the land it will be developing,” he said.
 Questions over infrastructure 
 Community groups acknowledged that a data centre could generate fewer daily vehicle trips than a large residential development, but said traffic alone should not determine whether it was suitable for the site.
 They want to know how much electricity and water a data centre would consume, whether existing utility networks could cope and whether its cooling equipment, generators and other machinery would generate excessive heat or noise close to homes.
 They also want assurance that development beside the pond would not reduce its storage capacity, obstruct water flow or undermine its flood mitigation function.
 Ng: Data centres should not be located in residential or commercial zones. 
 Joint Committee to Preserve the Bohol Flood Detention Pond spokesperson Datuk Ng See Eng said the suitability of the location and capacity of existing infrastructure needed scrutiny.
 “Data centres should not be located in residential or commercial zones. They are more suited to industrial areas.
 “However, the government currently allows data centres in commercial areas, sometimes very close to homes.
 “This is unfavourable to nearby residents.
 “We must also consider whether the existing infrastructure can cope with the additional demand.
 “Data centres consume large amounts of water and electricity, and that comes at an environmental cost,” he said.
 Low: Development cannot be determined simply by how much land is available. 
 Kuala Lumpur Residents Action for Sustainable Development Association (KLRA+SD) honorary secretary Joshua Low said the pond’s upgrading should strengthen the area’s flood resilience, not come with development that could place further pressure on its environment and infrastructure.
 “Development cannot be determined simply by how much land is available.
 “It must be guided by what the surrounding area and its infrastructure can sustainably support,” he said.
 Low said DBKL must first establish whether existing infrastructure could meet the additional water and electricity demand without compromising the needs of surrounding communities.
 He said power and water requirements of data centres, along with heat and noise from cooling systems and backup generators, raised legitimate concerns about locating one near high-density housing.
 “Residents should not have to bear the environmental consequences of having a resource-
 intensive facility placed next to their homes,” he said, adding that DBKL must look at all factors before approving such a development.
 Ali wants proposal presented to surrounding communities before planning approval is granted. 
 Save Kuala Lumpur chairman Datuk M. Ali said the project’s impact would depend on its size, cooling system and power requirements, as well as whether it would use treated or recycled water or another source.
 He called on the authorities and utility providers to disclose projected water and electricity consumption, the capacity of existing networks and any upgrades that would be needed.
 Ali also said the proposal should be presented to surrounding communities before planning approval was granted.
 “Pushing for a data centre instead of housing doesn’t automatically make it better for us.
 “We need to know how much water and electricity it will used, what the noise will be like and whether the flood pond will still work properly.
 “If those answers aren’t clear, residents have every reason to be worried,” he said.
 Data centre growth 
 Data centre development is already gathering pace in the Malaysian capital.
 DBKL has received several applications from developers, while construction for such centres is underway in Bukit Jalil, including at Technology Park Malaysia.
 Other developments remain at proposal stage, including MRCB’s RM2.1bil artificial intelligence-ready data centre in Bukit Jalil.
 StarMetro also learnt that DBKL sent a team of planners to Johor in July to study data centre developments and learn from the state’s experience in managing the rapidly growing industry.
 Johor has emerged as one of the fastest growing data centre hubs in the region, with many more projects, like this one located at the SiLC industrial park in Iskandar Puteri, in the works. — Filepic 
 However, there has been growing concern among the public over the increasing number of resource-hungry data centres, especially those situated near residential or commercial areas.
 Digital Minister Gobind Singh Deo said public concerns over the impact of data centres on energy and water resources were legitimate and must be addressed.
 Speaking at the launch of National Artificial Intelligence Readiness Week 2026 in Ampang last week, Gobind said data centres consumed significant amounts of energy and water.
 “In the next quarter, we may table the Data Infrastructure Act in Parliament.
 The Sungai Kuyoh inlet channels excess river water into Kampung Bohol Flood Detention Pond during heavy rain. It is one of several upgrades to the pond. 
 “One of the things I want to address through this legislation is precisely this issue,” he said.
 Last Friday, Investment, Trade and Industry (Miti) Minister Datuk Seri Johari Abdul Ghani said in a parliamentary reply that mandatory disclosure of data centre information, including power usage and the number of imported graphics processing unit (GPU) chips, would be embedded in law to enable closer monitoring.
 According to Miti, 55 of the 117 approved data centre projects in Malaysia had begun operations.
 Johari said the government needed details on operators, hyperscalers and locations for each facility.
 He added that operators must determine their actual power capacity needs, as utility suppliers were bound to allocate the exact capacity stipulated in their agreements.
 For the Kampung Bohol site, however, any formal scrutiny under these upcoming rules hinges on whether the developer proceeds with submitting a land-use conversion application to DBKL.
